```{python}
#| label: arr-salgo-a7-demo
A7_THRESHOLD = 16

def a7_introsort(a, naive_pivot=False, depth_limit=True, stats=None):
    """Quicksort (median of 3, Hoare) + depth limit -> heapsort; final insertion pass."""
    a, n = list(a), len(a)
    stats = {} if stats is None else stats
    stats["heap"] = 0

    def median3(i, j, k):
        if a[i] < a[j]:
            if a[j] < a[k]: return j
            return k if a[i] < a[k] else i
        if a[i] < a[k]: return i
        return k if a[j] < a[k] else j

    def partition(lo, hi):                         # Hoare, pivot a[lo]: a[lo..j] <= x <= a[j+1..hi]
        x, i, j = a[lo], lo - 1, hi + 1
        while True:
            i += 1
            while a[i] < x: i += 1
            j -= 1
            while a[j] > x: j -= 1
            if i >= j: return j
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]

    def loop(lo, hi, depth):                       # works on a[lo:hi]
        while hi - lo > A7_THRESHOLD:
            if depth == 0:
                a[lo:hi] = a5_heapsort(a[lo:hi])   # (C++ does this in place)
                stats["heap"] += 1
                return
            depth -= 1
            m = lo if naive_pivot else median3(lo, (lo + hi) // 2, hi - 1)
            a[lo], a[m] = a[m], a[lo]
            cut = partition(lo, hi - 1) + 1
            if cut - lo < hi - cut:                # smaller side recursively, larger in the loop
                loop(lo, cut, depth); lo = cut
            else:
                loop(cut, hi, depth); hi = cut

    loop(0, n, 2 * (n.bit_length() - 1) if (depth_limit and n) else float("inf"))
    stats["final_shifts"] = a1_shifts(a)
    return a1_insertion(a)

a7_witness = a0_check(a7_introsort, stable=False)
for _ in range(100):
    st, arr = {}, [random.randint(0, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 300))]
    assert a7_introsort(arr, stats=st) == sorted(arr)
    assert st["final_shifts"] < max(1, len(arr)) * A7_THRESHOLD    # the final pass is O(n)
n, st = 300, {}
a7_guarded = a0_comparisons(lambda b: a7_introsort(b, naive_pivot=True, stats=st), list(range(n)))
a7_plain = a0_comparisons(lambda b: a7_introsort(b, naive_pivot=True, depth_limit=False), list(range(n)))
assert st["heap"] >= 1                              # first-element pivot on sorted input: fallback fires
assert a7_guarded <= 4 * n * math.log2(n) and a7_plain > n * n // 3   # O(n log n) versus quadratic
assert a0_comparisons(a7_introsort, random.sample(range(10**6), 1000)) <= 2 * 1000 * math.log2(1000)
print(f"a7 introsort OK: sorted input, first-element pivot: {a7_guarded} comparisons with the "
      f"depth limit, {a7_plain} without")
```

#### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
const int THRESHOLD = 16;
int heapFallbacks = 0;

int median3(vector<int>& a, int i, int j, int k) {
    if (a[i] < a[j]) return a[j] < a[k] ? j : (a[i] < a[k] ? k : i);
    return a[i] < a[k] ? i : (a[j] < a[k] ? k : j);
}

// Hoare partition with the pivot at a[lo]; returns j with a[lo..j] <= x <= a[j+1..hi], lo <= j < hi.
int hoareFront(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi) {
    int x = a[lo], i = lo - 1, j = hi + 1;
    while (true) {
        do ++i; while (a[i] < x);
        do --j; while (a[j] > x);
        if (i >= j) return j;
        swap(a[i], a[j]);
    }
}

// Sort a[lo, hi) down to unsorted blocks of <= THRESHOLD elements, in the right block order.
void introLoop(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi, int depth, bool naive) {
    while (hi - lo > THRESHOLD) {
        if (depth == 0) {                                       // too many bad splits: heapsort this range
            make_heap(a.begin() + lo, a.begin() + hi);
            sort_heap(a.begin() + lo, a.begin() + hi);
            ++heapFallbacks;
            return;
        }
        --depth;
        int m = naive ? lo : median3(a, lo, lo + (hi - lo) / 2, hi - 1);
        swap(a[lo], a[m]);
        int cut = hoareFront(a, lo, hi - 1) + 1;
        if (cut - lo < hi - cut) { introLoop(a, lo, cut, depth, naive); lo = cut; }
        else                     { introLoop(a, cut, hi, depth, naive); hi = cut; }
    }
}

void introSort(vector<int>& a, bool naive = false) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    if (n < 2) return;
    int lg = 31 - __builtin_clz(n);                              // floor(log2 n)
    introLoop(a, 0, n, 2 * lg, naive);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) {                                // one final insertion pass
        int key = a[i], j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) { a[j + 1] = a[j]; --j; }
        a[j + 1] = key;
    }
}

int main() {
    mt19937 rng(8);
    for (int t = 0; t < 2000; ++t) {
        int n = rng() % 400, spread = t % 2 ? 3 : 100000;
        vector<int> a(n);
        for (int& x : a) x = (int)(rng() % (2 * spread + 1)) - spread;
        vector<int> want = a;
        sort(want.begin(), want.end());
        introSort(a, t % 5 == 0);
        assert(a == want);
    }
    vector<int> s(100000);
    iota(s.begin(), s.end(), 0);
    heapFallbacks = 0;
    introSort(s, true);                       // first-element pivot on sorted input: worst case for quicksort
    assert(is_sorted(s.begin(), s.end()) && heapFallbacks >= 1);
    printf("introsort OK (%d heapsort fallback on sorted input)\n", heapFallbacks);
}
```
:::

The experiment at the end of the Python tab is the point of the design. With a deliberately bad pivot rule (the first element) on sorted input, plain quicksort makes a quadratic number of comparisons; with the depth limit, the same code bails out to heapsort after $2\lfloor\log_2 300\rfloor = 16$ bad levels and stays within a small multiple of $n\log_2 n$.

## A8. Timsort: what Python's `sorted` runs {#sec-salgo-a8}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Real data is rarely random: it often contains stretches that are already in order (a sorted list with a few new items appended, two sorted lists glued together, a reversed block). Timsort finds these **runs**, reverses the descending ones, lengthens short runs to a minimum length with binary insertion sort, and merges neighbouring runs in a balanced order. It is a **stable**, **adaptive** merge sort: $n - 1$ comparisons on sorted input, $O(n\log n)$ in the worst case.
:::

Tim Peters wrote Timsort for Python in 2002, and `Objects/listsort.txt` in the CPython source describes it in detail. It is also used for object arrays in Java and for `Array.prototype.sort` in V8 (the JavaScript engine of Chrome and Node.js). Its parts:

1. **Runs.** Scan from the left for the longest prefix that is non-decreasing (`a[0] <= a[1] <= ...`) or *strictly* decreasing (`a[0] > a[1] > ...`). A strictly decreasing run is reversed in place; strictness matters, because reversing a run that contains equal keys would swap their order and break stability.
2. **Minrun.** Very short runs would make many tiny merges, so a run shorter than `minrun` is extended to `minrun` elements (or to the end of the array) with binary insertion sort (@sec-salgo-a1). For $n < 64$, `minrun` $= n$: the whole array is one binary insertion sort. Otherwise `minrun` lies between 32 and 64, chosen so that $n/\text{minrun}$ is a power of two or just below one, which keeps the merges balanced. (The classic rule takes the six leading bits of $n$ and adds 1 if any other bit is set; recent CPython versions refine it so that run lengths differ by at most one.)
3. **The merge stack.** Each new run is pushed on a stack of pending runs, and neighbouring runs are merged until the stack satisfies a balance invariant. In the original design the lengths $A, B, C$ of the three topmost runs must satisfy $A > B + C$ and $B > C$, so lengths grow at least like Fibonacci numbers down the stack and the stack has $O(\log n)$ runs. (In 2015 de Gouw and others found, while trying to verify Java's port formally, that the original check did not always restore the invariant; the fix checks one more level. Current CPython chooses merges with the "powersort" rule of Munro and Wild instead.) Only *neighbouring* runs are ever merged, which is what keeps the sort stable.
4. **Galloping.** When one run keeps winning the merge (seven times in a row at first; the threshold adapts), the merge switches to an exponential search for where the other run's head belongs and copies the whole block at once. Merging a short run into a long one then costs about $O(\text{short} \cdot \log \text{long})$ comparisons instead of $O(\text{short} + \text{long})$.

**Cost.** Run detection makes about one comparison per element. On sorted (or strictly decreasing) input there is a single run and no merge, so the sort costs exactly $n - 1$ comparisons. With $\rho$ runs of similar length the merges form a balanced tree of depth $\log_2 \rho$, so the cost is about $n\log_2 \rho$: few runs, nearly linear. On random data all runs are boosted to `minrun` and Timsort behaves like a well-balanced merge sort, $O(n\log n)$ (a 2018 analysis by Auger, Jugé, Nicaud and Pivoteau proved the worst case $O(n\log n)$ for the repaired merge rule). Merges copy the smaller of the two runs into a temporary buffer, so the extra memory is at most $n/2$ elements.

| Input | Comparisons | Extra space |
|---|---|---|
| sorted or strictly decreasing | $n - 1$ | $O(1)$ |
| $\rho$ balanced runs | about $n\log_2 \rho$ | $\le n/2$ |
| random (worst) | $O(n\log n)$ | $\le n/2$ |

**Stable** and **adaptive**; not in place.

The version below ("Timsort-lite") has runs, minrun, binary insertion and the repaired stack invariant, but merges without galloping. It checks the stack invariant after every push, sorts like `sorted`, is stable, and makes $n - 1$ comparisons on sorted and on reversed input.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-salgo-a8-demo
def a8_minrun(n):
    """Classic rule: n < 64 -> n; else the top 6 bits of n, plus 1 if any lower bit is set."""
    r = 0
    while n >= 64:
        r |= n & 1
        n >>= 1
    return n + r

def a8_count_run(a, lo, n):
    """Length of the run at lo; a strictly descending run is reversed in place."""
    hi = lo + 1
    if hi == n:
        return 1
    if a[hi] < a[lo]:                                   # strictly descending
        while hi + 1 < n and a[hi + 1] < a[hi]:
            hi += 1
        a[lo:hi + 1] = a[lo:hi + 1][::-1]
    else:                                               # non-descending
        while hi + 1 < n and not a[hi + 1] < a[hi]:
            hi += 1
    return hi - lo + 1

def a8_binary_insertion(a, lo, hi, start):
    """a[lo:start] is sorted; insert a[start:hi] one by one (stable: bisect_right)."""
    for i in range(start, hi):
        x = a[i]
        pos = bisect_right(a, x, lo, i)
        a[pos + 1:i + 1] = a[pos:i]
        a[pos] = x

def a8_merge_at(a, runs, i):
    (s1, n1), (s2, n2) = runs[i], runs[i + 1]
    a[s1:s2 + n2] = a3_merge(a[s1:s2], a[s2:s2 + n2])  # neighbours only: stable
    runs[i] = (s1, n1 + n2)
    del runs[i + 1]

def a8_merge_collapse(a, runs):
    """Merge until, from the top, lengths satisfy A > B + C and B > C (repaired check)."""
    while len(runs) > 1:
        n = len(runs) - 2
        L = [r[1] for r in runs]
        if (n > 0 and L[n - 1] <= L[n] + L[n + 1]) or (n > 1 and L[n - 2] <= L[n - 1] + L[n]):
            if L[n - 1] < L[n + 1]:
                n -= 1
            a8_merge_at(a, runs, n)
        elif L[n] <= L[n + 1]:
            a8_merge_at(a, runs, n)
        else:
            break

def a8_timsort(a, stats=None):
    a, n = list(a), len(a)
    stats = {} if stats is None else stats
    stats.update(runs=0, max_stack=0)
    if n < 2:
        return a
    minrun, runs, lo = a8_minrun(n), [], 0
    while lo < n:
        length = a8_count_run(a, lo, n)
        if length < minrun:                             # boost a short run to minrun
            force = min(minrun, n - lo)
            a8_binary_insertion(a, lo, lo + force, lo + length)
            length = force
        runs.append((lo, length))
        stats["runs"] += 1
        a8_merge_collapse(a, runs)
        L = [r[1] for r in runs]                        # the invariant, checked every time
        assert all(L[k] > L[k + 1] for k in range(len(L) - 1))
        assert all(L[k] > L[k + 1] + L[k + 2] for k in range(len(L) - 2))
        stats["max_stack"] = max(stats["max_stack"], len(runs))
        lo += length
    while len(runs) > 1:                                # final collapse, top down
        k = len(runs) - 2
        if k > 0 and runs[k - 1][1] < runs[k + 1][1]:
            k -= 1
        a8_merge_at(a, runs, k)
    return a

for n in list(range(1, 200)) + [1000, 4096, 4097, 10**5]:
    m = a8_minrun(n)
    assert m == n if n < 64 else 32 <= m <= 64
a0_check(a8_timsort, stable=True)
for _ in range(50):
    arr = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 3000))]
    assert a8_timsort(arr) == sorted(arr)
for n in (5, 64, 1000):                                 # one run: n - 1 comparisons
    assert a0_comparisons(a8_timsort, list(range(n))) == n - 1
    assert a0_comparisons(a8_timsort, list(range(n, 0, -1))) == n - 1
a8_four = [x for _ in range(4) for x in sorted(random.sample(range(10**6), 1024))]
assert a0_comparisons(a8_timsort, a8_four) <= 3 * len(a8_four)     # 4 runs: two merge levels
a8_stats = {}
a8_timsort(random.sample(range(10**6), 20000), a8_stats)
assert a8_stats["max_stack"] <= 2 * math.log2(20000)               # the stack stays logarithmic
print("a8 timsort-lite OK:", a8_stats)
```

#### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
using Item = pair<int, int>;                       // (key, input index); only the key is compared
bool lessKey(const Item& x, const Item& y) { return x.first < y.first; }

int minRun(int n) {                                // classic rule: n < 64 -> n, else in [32, 64]
    int r = 0;
    while (n >= 64) { r |= n & 1; n >>= 1; }
    return n + r;
}

// Length of the run at lo; a strictly descending run is reversed (strict, so reversing is stable).
int countRun(vector<Item>& a, int lo, int n) {
    int hi = lo + 1;
    if (hi == n) return 1;
    if (lessKey(a[hi], a[lo])) {
        while (hi + 1 < n && lessKey(a[hi + 1], a[hi])) ++hi;
        reverse(a.begin() + lo, a.begin() + hi + 1);
    } else {
        while (hi + 1 < n && !lessKey(a[hi + 1], a[hi])) ++hi;
    }
    return hi - lo + 1;
}

void binaryInsertion(vector<Item>& a, int lo, int hi, int start) {   // a[lo, start) is sorted
    for (int i = start; i < hi; ++i) {
        auto pos = upper_bound(a.begin() + lo, a.begin() + i, a[i], lessKey);
        rotate(pos, a.begin() + i, a.begin() + i + 1);
    }
}

struct Run { int start, len; };

void mergeAt(vector<Item>& a, vector<Run>& runs, int i) {           // merge runs i and i+1
    Run x = runs[i], y = runs[i + 1];
    vector<Item> tmp(a.begin() + x.start, a.begin() + x.start + x.len);   // copy the left run out
    merge(tmp.begin(), tmp.end(), a.begin() + y.start, a.begin() + y.start + y.len,
          a.begin() + x.start, lessKey);                             // std::merge is stable
    runs[i].len += y.len;
    runs.erase(runs.begin() + i + 1);
}

void mergeCollapse(vector<Item>& a, vector<Run>& runs) {             // keep run lengths shrinking fast
    while (runs.size() > 1) {
        int n = (int)runs.size() - 2;
        if ((n > 0 && runs[n - 1].len <= runs[n].len + runs[n + 1].len) ||
            (n > 1 && runs[n - 2].len <= runs[n - 1].len + runs[n].len)) {
            if (runs[n - 1].len < runs[n + 1].len) --n;
            mergeAt(a, runs, n);
        } else if (runs[n].len <= runs[n + 1].len) {
            mergeAt(a, runs, n);
        } else break;
    }
}

void timSortLite(vector<Item>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    if (n < 2) return;
    int mr = minRun(n), lo = 0;
    vector<Run> runs;
    while (lo < n) {
        int len = countRun(a, lo, n);
        if (len < mr) {                                              // boost a short run to minrun
            int force = min(mr, n - lo);
            binaryInsertion(a, lo, lo + force, lo + len);
            len = force;
        }
        runs.push_back({lo, len});
        mergeCollapse(a, runs);
        lo += len;
    }
    while (runs.size() > 1) {                                        // final collapse
        int n2 = (int)runs.size() - 2;
        if (n2 > 0 && runs[n2 - 1].len < runs[n2 + 1].len) --n2;
        mergeAt(a, runs, n2);
    }
}

int main() {
    mt19937 rng(9);
    for (int t = 0; t < 600; ++t) {
        int n = rng() % 3000;
        vector<Item> a(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) a[i] = {(int)(rng() % (t % 2 ? 7 : 100000)), i};
        if (t % 7 == 0) sort(a.begin(), a.begin() + n / 2, lessKey);  // partly presorted
        vector<Item> want = a;
        stable_sort(want.begin(), want.end(), lessKey);
        timSortLite(a);
        assert(a == want);                                            // sorted and stable
    }
    puts("timsort-lite OK");
}
```
:::

Here are the runs that `a8_count_run` finds on a small example:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def a8_runs_draw(ax, p):
    src = [3, 5, 8, 9, 7, 4, 2, 6, 6, 10, 12, 1]
    a, lo, regions, names = list(src), 0, [], ["run 1", "run 2", "run 3", "run 4"]
    while lo < len(a):
        before = a[lo:lo + 2]
        length = a8_count_run(a, lo, len(a))
        kind = "desc, reversed" if len(before) == 2 and before[1] < before[0] else "asc"
        regions.append((lo, lo + length, ["indigo", "amber", "cyan", "violet"][len(regions)],
                        f"{names[len(regions)]}: {kind}" if length > 1 else names[len(regions)]))
        lo += length
    assert a == [3, 5, 8, 9, 2, 4, 7, 6, 6, 10, 12, 1] and len(regions) == 4
    V.array(ax, p, src, y=2.6, label="input")
    V.array(ax, p, a, y=0.0, label="runs", regions=regions)
V.show(a8_runs_draw)
```

Natural runs of $[3,5,8,9,7,4,2,6,6,10,12,1]$, found by the same `count_run` the code below uses. The strictly descending run $7,4,2$ is reversed in place; $6,6,10,12$ is a non-decreasing run (equal neighbours are allowed in ascending runs). For an array this short, real Timsort would then binary-insertion-sort everything, because $n < 64$.

:::

**When it is used.** Whenever stability is required or the data is likely to be partly ordered: Python's `sorted` and `list.sort`, Java's `Arrays.sort` for objects and `Collections.sort`, and JavaScript's `Array.prototype.sort` in V8. Its weakness is the $n/2$ buffer and slightly more data movement than quicksort on random data, which is why C++ keeps an unstable introsort as its default.

## A9. Choosing a sort {#sec-salgo-a9}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
There is no best sort, only a best sort for a situation. Ask four questions: do I need **stability**? Is the data **already partly sorted**? Can I afford **$O(n)$ extra memory**? Do I need a **worst-case** guarantee? The table answers them; the figure measures them.
:::

| Sort | Best | Average | Worst | Extra space | Stable | Adaptive | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insertion (@sec-salgo-a1) | $n$ | $n^2$ | $n^2$ | $O(1)$ | yes | yes | tiny or nearly sorted arrays; the finisher in hybrids |
| Selection (@sec-salgo-a2) | $n^2$ | $n^2$ | $n^2$ | $O(1)$ | no | no | when writes are expensive (at most $n-1$ swaps) |
| Merge (@sec-salgo-a3) | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $O(n)$ | yes | no | stable sorting, linked lists, external sorting |
| Quicksort (@sec-salgo-a4) | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $n^2$ | $O(\log n)$ | no | no | fast in-memory sorting (inside introsort) |
| Heapsort (@sec-salgo-a5) | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $O(1)$ | no | no | worst-case guarantee in $O(1)$ memory; fallback |
| Introsort (@sec-salgo-a7) | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $O(\log n)$ | no | little | C++ `std::sort` |
| Timsort (@sec-salgo-a8) | $n$ | $n\log n$ | $n\log n$ | $O(n)$ | yes | yes | Python, Java objects, V8 |

All entries are $\Theta(\cdot)$ time bounds (quicksort's average is with a random pivot). The comparison-model floor is $\Omega(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a6); counting, radix and bucket sort escape it by not comparing (@sec-lts).

::: {#fig-salgo-a9}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
a9_n = 256
a9_inputs = {"random": random.sample(range(10**6), a9_n), "sorted": list(range(a9_n)),
             "reversed": list(range(a9_n, 0, -1)), "4 keys": [random.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(a9_n)],
             "all equal": [7] * a9_n}
a9_sorts = {"insertion": a1_insertion, "selection": a2_selection, "merge": a3_merge_sort,
            "quick (Lomuto)": a4_quicksort, "quick (3-way)": a4_quicksort3, "heapsort": a5_heapsort,
            "introsort": a7_introsort, "timsort-lite": a8_timsort}
a9_ref = a9_n * math.log2(a9_n)
a9_cells, a9_colors = [], {}
for r, fn in enumerate(a9_sorts.values()):
    row = []
    for c, data in enumerate(a9_inputs.values()):
        cmp = a0_comparisons(fn, data)
        row.append(str(cmp))
        a9_colors[(r, c)] = "green" if cmp <= 1.5 * a9_ref else ("amber" if cmp <= 4 * a9_ref else "red")
    a9_cells.append(row)
assert a9_cells[0][1] == str(a9_n - 1) and a9_cells[7][1] == str(a9_n - 1)      # adaptive on sorted
assert a9_colors[(3, 4)] == "red" and a9_colors[(4, 4)] == "green"               # Lomuto vs 3-way, equal keys

def a9_draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, a9_cells, row_labels=list(a9_sorts), col_labels=list(a9_inputs), cell_w=1.7, size=10)
V.show(a9_draw)
```

Comparisons made by each sort of this chapter on $n = 256$ keys, measured with the counting harness of @sec-salgo-a0. Green is at most $1.5\,n\log_2 n$ (here $n\log_2 n = 2048$), amber at most $4\,n\log_2 n$, red above. Read down a column to choose for a known input shape: insertion sort and Timsort are nearly free on sorted input, Lomuto quicksort collapses on all-equal keys while the three-way partition finishes them in one pass, and only the quadratic sorts turn red on random data.

:::

A practical decision list:

- **Just sorting in a contest or at work:** call the library (`sorted`, `std::sort`). Need stability in C++? `std::stable_sort`.
- **Need stability yourself:** merge sort (or any sort on `(key, index)` pairs).
- **Linked list:** merge sort, by relinking (@sec-salgo-p1-c).
- **Hard memory limit and a hard time limit:** heapsort.
- **Only the $k$-th element, or the $k$ smallest:** do not sort; quickselect or a heap (@sec-salgo-p3, @sec-salgo-p4).
- **Small integer keys:** counting or radix sort (@sec-lts).

## Part B — Patterns {#sec-salgo-partb}

Each pattern opens with the signals that say "use me", a boxed template with its invariant, and its complexity; then come its solved problems. Every problem has a full statement, a brute-force form and a refined form with matching C++, and stress tests against the brute force; most also have trace boards recorded by *running* the code.

## Pattern 1: Implement a comparison sort from scratch {#sec-salgo-p1}

**Where we are.** Part A built the sorts; Part B spends them. P1 is the raw skill: sort *by hand*, with no library call, on an array and then on a linked list, where the lack of random access decides which sort survives. P2 keeps merge sort's split but makes the merge *count* while it sorts. P3 drops the promise to order everything and keeps only quicksort's partition to select one rank. P4 replaces a one-off batch with a stream and keeps only a heap of the $k$ best. P5 stops asking "which order" and asks what the order does with ties.

**Recognise it.** "Sort the array **without any built-in sort**, in $O(n\log n)$, with as little extra space as possible"; "sort a **linked list**"; "sort it in place with at most $k$ swaps". These problems *are* the sorting algorithm, so they are the cleanest place to practise A1–A5, their invariants and their edge cases.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Pick the sort by the constraint that bites, then prove its invariant.

```text
array, O(n log n), stable or simple:   merge sort (top-down or bottom-up)        O(n) extra
array, O(1) extra, worst-case bound:   heapsort: build max-heap; swap root to end; sift down
linked list:                           insertion by relinking (O(n^2)), or merge sort by relinking
                                       (split with slow/fast pointers; bottom-up for O(1) extra)
```

**Invariant.** Every form keeps "a sorted region that only grows" (prefix for insertion/selection, suffix for heapsort) or "each recursive call returns a sorted permutation of its input" (merge sort).
:::

**Complexity.** Insertion and selection $O(n^2)$, merge sort $O(n\log n)$ with $O(n)$ extra on arrays, heapsort $O(n\log n)$ with $O(1)$ extra; on lists, merge sort is $O(n\log n)$ with $O(\log n)$ stack (top-down) or $O(1)$ (bottom-up).

{{< include ../problems/lc-0912-sort-an-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From an array to a chain.** LC 912 lets you index anywhere. A linked list allows only "next": no binary search for the slot, no swapping by index. The first sort to try on a chain is insertion sort, and the shift that cost $O(n)$ moves on an array becomes a single relink.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0147-insertion-sort-list/problem.qmd >}}

[**From quadratic to $n\log n$ on a chain.** Insertion sort by relinking is still $O(n^2)$ on a reversed list. Of the $n\log n$ sorts, quicksort's partition and heapsort's index arithmetic need random access, but merge sort only walks forward: split with slow and fast pointers, merge by relinking.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0148-sort-list/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 2: Count across the merge {#sec-salgo-p2}

**From sorting to counting with a merge.** Pattern 1 used the merge only to build order. While it stitches two *sorted* halves together it also learns, for free, how elements of the left half compare with elements of the right half, and every pair $(i, j)$ with $i$ in the left half and $j$ in the right half has $i < j$ in the original array. So a question like "how many pairs $i < j$ have $a_i > a_j$?" costs $O(n^2)$ by brute force and $O(n\log n)$ once the merge tallies the crossings.

**Recognise it.** "Count pairs $(i, j)$ with $i < j$ and [a comparison of $a_i$ with $a_j$]": inversions, crossings of wires, "smaller numbers after self", "$a_i > 2a_j$", "the minimum number of adjacent swaps to sort". The signal is a predicate that is **monotone** in each value, so that inside sorted runs it can be counted with one advancing pointer. $n$ up to $10^5$ rules out the pair scan.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Recurse for the pairs inside each half; count the pairs across the halves while (or just before) merging.

```text
sort_count(lo, hi):
    if hi - lo <= 1: return 0
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    c = sort_count(lo, mid) + sort_count(mid, hi)      # both halves now sorted
    c += cross(lo, mid, hi)                             # one forward pointer, O(hi - lo)
    merge a[lo:mid] and a[mid:hi]                       # stable merge, O(hi - lo)
    return c
```

**Invariant.** After the two recursive calls both halves are sorted and every within-half pair has been counted; every remaining pair crosses the midpoint, and because both halves are sorted the predicate can be tallied with pointers that only move forward. Sort *indices* instead of values when the answer must be reported per original position.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ extra space: the merge sort cost plus $O(1)$ per element per level for the tally. The pair scan is the $O(n^2)$ oracle.

{{< include ../problems/cf-1676h2-maximum-crossings-hard-version/problem.qmd >}}

[**From one total to a count per element.** CF 1676H2 needs only the number of inverted pairs. LC 315 asks, for *every* position, how many smaller elements lie to its right, so the merge must sort indices and credit each count to the element's original position.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0315-count-of-smaller-numbers-after-self/problem.qmd >}}

[**From `nums[i] > nums[j]` to `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]`.** Same divide and conquer, but now the predicate is not the merge's own comparison, so the crossing count becomes a separate two-pointer pass before the merge, and the doubling needs 64-bit care.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0493-reverse-pairs/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 3: Select a rank without a full sort {#sec-salgo-p3}

**From ordering everything to answering one rank.** Merge sort places *every* element; quicksort's partition places only the **pivot** at its final index and leaves each side unordered. If you only need the $k$-th element, that is all the promise you need: recurse into the single side holding the target and drop the other (@sec-salgo-a4-select). When the data is already ordered by structure (a matrix with sorted rows and columns) you cannot index by rank at all, and the trick becomes binary searching the *value* with a monotone count instead.

**Recognise it.** "The $k$-th largest/smallest", "the median", "the $k$ smallest values in any order", often with a "without sorting" follow-up. $n$ up to $10^5$ makes a full sort legal but wasteful; the follow-up is the hint to select.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
Partition, read the pivot's rank, keep one side.

```text
quickselect, target index t (k-th largest: t = n - k):
    partition a[lo..hi] three ways around a random pivot x: [< x | == x | > x] at [lo..lt-1 | lt..gt | gt+1..hi]
    t < lt: hi = lt - 1     t > gt: lo = gt + 1     else: return x
pre-ordered structure (sorted rows and columns): binary search the value v, count(<= v) per row
```

**Invariant.** The answer's index $t$ always lies in `[lo, hi]`, and after a partition every element left of the `== x` block is smaller and every element right of it is larger, so discarding the side without $t$ never discards the answer.
:::

**Complexity.** Quickselect expected $O(n)$, worst case $O(n^2)$, $O(1)$ extra. Binary search on the value over an $n\times n$ matrix costs $O(n\log(\text{range}))$ with a staircase count. A full sort, $O(n\log n)$, is the oracle.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0215-kth-largest-element-in-an-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a flat array to a sorted matrix.** Quickselect needs to move elements around by index. A matrix whose rows and columns are sorted already contains a lot of order, but you cannot partition it or index it by rank; binary search over the *value*, with a monotone "how many cells $\le x$" count, selects the rank without moving anything.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0378-kth-smallest-element-in-a-sorted-matrix/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 4: Keep a heap for top-k {#sec-salgo-p4}

**From one rank to a running set of k.** Pattern 3 answered a *single* rank once, over data held in memory all at once. Ask instead for "the best $k$", or let the data **stream** in so that history cannot be re-scanned, and the right structure is the binary heap of @sec-salgo-a5: a heap capped at $k$ elements gives top-$k$ in $O(n\log k)$, and its root is the current $k$-th best, readable in $O(1)$ after every arrival.

**Recognise it.** "The $k$ closest / $k$ most frequent / top $k$"; "the $k$-th largest **in a stream**" (a class with an `add`); "merge $k$ sorted lists"; anything where $k \ll n$ makes paying $\log n$ per element wasteful.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
A bounded heap is a running top-$k$; its root is the eviction threshold.

```text
k smallest of a batch:   max-heap of size k (Python: push -key); pop when size > k   -> the k survivors
k-th largest of stream:  min-heap of size k; root = answer; add: push if size < k, else replace if val > root
k-way merge:             min-heap of the k current heads; pop the smallest, push its successor
```

**Invariant.** The heap holds exactly the $k$ best elements seen so far (or, for a $k$-way merge, the smallest unmerged element of each list); its root is the worst of them, so it is both the answer and the next element to evict.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n\log k)$ time and $O(k)$ space for $n$ elements, against $O(n\log n)$ and $O(n)$ to sort everything; $O(\log k)$ per stream update. Quickselect is the batch $O(n)$ alternative when everything fits in memory and the $k$ results may come out in any order.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0973-k-closest-points-to-origin/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a batch to a stream.** The $k$ closest points are fixed once you can see them all; when values arrive one by one and you must answer after each, you cannot re-sort. Keep the heap alive between queries, and the answer becomes its root.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-0703-kth-largest-element-in-a-stream/problem.qmd >}}

**The heap as a merge engine.** A heap can also *produce* sorted order from several sorted sources. Merging $k$ sorted lists keeps the $k$ current heads in a min-heap: pop the smallest, output it, push its successor. That is $O(N\log k)$ for $N$ elements in total, and it is exactly the inner loop of **external merge sort**: sort memory-sized chunks of a huge file, write each chunk out as a sorted run, then merge all runs in one streaming pass with a heap of $k$ heads. The problem is solved in full where heaps first appear:

{{< include ../problems/lc-0023-merge-k-sorted-lists/card.qmd >}}

Read it as the merge of @sec-salgo-a3 with the two-way "smaller head" test replaced by a heap of $k$ heads.

## Pattern 5: Stability and the direction of a tie-break {#sec-salgo-p5}

**From the order to what the order keeps.** The first four patterns used sortedness for its *value* order. Two facts about *how* the order is produced decide another family of problems. **Stability** says that elements that compare equal keep their input order (@sec-salgo-a6-stable); **tie-break direction** says, among equal primary keys, whether the secondary key ascends or descends. Each can be the difference between right and wrong.

**Recognise it.** A sort where a *group must not move relative to itself* ("the digit-logs keep their relative order", "equal elements keep their original order") points to stability. A multi-key sort followed by a sweep, where an element must not be "beaten" by an equal-key neighbour, points to a designed tie-break. Both feel like "the sort is easy, the order I want is subtle".

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
The key and the tie-break are the algorithm.

```text
keep one group fixed:     sort only the other group and concatenate, or one STABLE sort with key (group, ...)
several keys:             one tuple key (primary, secondary), or stable passes from least to most significant
ties must not dominate:   sort (primary ASC, secondary DESC), then sweep keeping a running max of secondary
```

**Invariant.** A stable sort never reorders items with equal keys; a chosen tie-break direction decides which equal-key items are adjacent, and therefore which ones a later sweep can see as strictly better.
:::

**Complexity.** $O(n\log n)$ comparisons; the design effort is in proving that the key is a strict weak ordering (@sec-srt-a2) and that the sort used is stable when stability is needed. These problems are cheap to code and expensive to get *right*.

{{< include ../problems/lc-0937-reorder-data-in-log-files/problem.qmd >}}

[**From "keep a group in order" to "make ties harmless".** LC 937 uses stability to freeze one group's order. LC 1996 pulls the opposite lever: it deliberately *reverses* the secondary key's direction so that characters with equal attack can never count as dominating each other in the sweep that follows. Same control over ties, opposite purpose.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-1996-the-number-of-weak-characters-in-the-game/problem.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** One idea ran through every lesson: *keep an invariant about a region that only grows*. Insertion and selection sort grow a sorted prefix one element at a time and pay $O(n^2)$ for it (A1, A2). Merge sort replaces "one element at a time" with "two sorted halves at a time", which is balanced by construction and gives $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, plus a merge that can count (A3, P1, P2). Quicksort does the work before recursing instead of after, and its partition, applied to one side only, selects a rank in expected linear time (A4, P3). Heapsort keeps selection sort's idea but answers "what is the maximum?" with a heap, which also powers top-$k$ and streams (A5, P4). The decision tree shows that $n\log n$ comparisons cannot be beaten (A6), so the libraries compete on everything else: introsort on the worst case, Timsort on existing order and stability (A7, A8), and stability itself becomes a tool (P5). The one way left to go faster is to stop comparing, which is the next chapter, @sec-lts.

## Pattern map

<!-- Copied into the Cheat Sheets appendix by gen_book.py: keep it one table, no labels. -->

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| "Sort without a built-in sort, $O(n\log n)$, least space" | Merge sort or heapsort by hand | @sec-salgo-p1-a |
| "Sort a linked list" (small $n$, or "insertion") | Insertion sort by relinking | @sec-salgo-p1-b |
| "Sort a linked list in $O(n\log n)$, $O(1)$ memory" | List merge sort, bottom-up | @sec-salgo-p1-c |
| "How many pairs $i<j$ with $a_i \ge a_j$" (inversions, crossings, adjacent swaps) | Count across the merge | @sec-salgo-p2-a |
| "For each $i$, how many smaller to its right" | Merge sort over indices | @sec-salgo-p2-b |
| Pairs with $a_i > 2a_j$ or another monotone predicate | Separate cross-count pass, 64-bit | @sec-salgo-p2-c |
| "The $k$-th largest/smallest", "median", once | Quickselect on the pivot's rank | @sec-salgo-p3-a |
| $k$-th smallest where rows and columns are sorted | Binary search the value, count $\le x$ | @sec-salgo-p3-b |
| "The $k$ closest / top $k$" of a batch | Bounded heap (or quickselect) | @sec-salgo-p4-a |
| "The $k$-th largest **in a stream**", an `add` with a running answer | Persistent size-$k$ heap | @sec-salgo-p4-b |
| "One group must keep its relative order" | Stability (or sort only the other group) | @sec-salgo-p5-a |
| Correctness hinges on how equal primary keys are ordered | Design the tie-break direction | @sec-salgo-p5-b |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **`>=` in insertion sort's shift test.** Shifting while `a[j] >= key` moves equal keys past each other and loses stability (and does extra work). Shift only while strictly greater (@sec-salgo-a1).
- **A strict `<` for the left head in a merge.** Taking the right head on ties (`L[i] < R[j]` for the left) makes merge sort unstable. Take the left head when `L[i] <= R[j]` (@sec-salgo-a3).
- **A fixed pivot on sorted input.** Always choosing `a[hi]` (or `a[lo]`) splits sorted data $0 \mid n-1$ and runs in $\Theta(n^2)$, with $\Theta(n)$ recursion depth. Randomise the pivot or use median-of-three, and recurse into the smaller side (@sec-salgo-a4).
- **Lomuto's partition on many equal keys.** Every element is $\le$ the pivot, so the split is $n-1 \mid 0$ again. Use Hoare's partition, which stops on equal keys, or the three-way partition (@sec-salgo-a4-hoare).
- **Hoare's partition with the pivot at `a[hi]`.** With the classic code the returned $j$ can equal `hi`, so the recursion on `[lo..j]` never shrinks. Take the pivot from the middle (or the front), as in @sec-salgo-a4-hoare.
- **Off-by-one in heap indices.** With 0-based arrays the children of $i$ are $2i+1$ and $2i+2$ and the last internal node is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor - 1$; the 1-based formulas $2i, 2i+1$ silently skip or duplicate nodes (@sec-salgo-a5).
- **Building a heap with $n$ pushes and calling it $O(n)$.** Repeated `push` is $O(n\log n)$; bottom-up sift-down (`heapify`, `make_heap`) is $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a5-build).
- **Assuming `std::sort` is stable.** It is introsort and is not stable; use `std::stable_sort`, or a tuple key, when input order inside ties matters (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-p5-a).
- **Reversing a non-strictly descending run.** A run like $5, 3, 3, 1$ reversed in place swaps the two $3$s; Timsort only reverses *strictly* descending runs (@sec-salgo-a8).
- **Counting crossings with a nested loop.** Once both halves are sorted, the cross count is one forward pointer; re-scanning is the $O(n^2)$ you came to avoid (@sec-salgo-p2-a, @sec-salgo-p2-c).
- **`2 * nums[j]` in 32-bit.** For values near $2^{31}$ the doubling overflows; widen to `long long` first (@sec-salgo-p2-c).
- **Sorting a linked list with quicksort or heapsort.** No random access means no index-based partition and no `2i+1` children; use merge sort by relinking (@sec-salgo-p1-c).
- **Re-sorting the whole pool per stream query.** That makes each `add` $O(n\log n)$; a size-$k$ heap makes it $O(\log k)$ (@sec-salgo-p4-b).
- **Wrong tie-break direction on dominance.** Sorting `(attack, defense)` both ascending lets an equal-attack character "dominate" its peer; `(attack ASC, defense DESC)` is what makes the right-to-left sweep correct (@sec-salgo-p5-b).
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E] Write insertion sort and state its exact inner-loop condition. Why must that comparison be strict (`>`) rather than `>=` for the sort to be stable?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Shift `a[j]` right only while `a[j] > key`. If the test were `>=`, an element equal to `key` would also be shifted, so `key` would land *before* an equal element that came first in the input, breaking input order. The strict test stops at the first equal element and drops `key` right after it (@sec-salgo-a1).
:::

**2. [E] On `a = [5, 2, 4, 1, 3]` count the total number of shifts made by insertion sort and the total number of swaps made by selection sort. Relate the shift count to inversions.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The inversions of $[5,2,4,1,3]$ are $(5,2),(5,4),(5,1),(5,3),(2,1),(4,1),(4,3)$, seven of them, and insertion sort makes exactly $7$ shifts: each shift moves one element past a smaller key that was behind it, which removes one inversion. Selection sort swaps at most once per pass: pass 0 swaps $1$ to the front ($[1,2,4,5,3]$), pass 1 finds $2$ in place, pass 2 swaps $3$ in ($[1,2,3,5,4]$), pass 3 swaps $4$ in: $3$ swaps, never more than $n - 1 = 4$. So insertion sort costs $O(n + \text{inversions})$ while selection sort's writes stay $O(n)$ on every input (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a2).
:::

**3. [E] Bubble sort repeatedly sweeps the array and swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs. Prove that it makes exactly as many swaps as there are inversions, and give its best and worst number of sweeps (with the "stop when a sweep makes no swap" rule).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Swapping an adjacent pair $a_i > a_{i+1}$ removes exactly that one inversion and changes no other pair's relative order, so each swap lowers the inversion count by exactly one; the array is sorted when the count is $0$, hence #swaps $=$ #inversions. After sweep $k$ the $k$ largest elements are in their final places (each sweep carries the maximum of the unsorted part to its end), so at most $n - 1$ sweeps are needed (a reversed array); on a sorted array the first sweep makes no swap and the algorithm stops after one sweep, $n - 1$ comparisons. Like insertion sort it is stable (it never swaps equal neighbours), but it does more comparisons and writes, so insertion sort is preferred (@sec-salgo-a0, @sec-salgo-a1).
:::

**4. [M] Give an input on which quicksort with a last-element pivot runs in $\Theta(n^2)$ while merge sort stays $\Theta(n\log n)$, and explain what randomising the pivot does and does not guarantee.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A sorted array: the last element is always the maximum, so every partition splits $n-1 \mid 0$ and the comparisons are $(n-1) + (n-2) + \dots = \binom n2$. Merge sort splits in the middle whatever the input, so it stays $\Theta(n\log n)$. With a random pivot *every* input has expected cost $2(n+1)H_n - 4n \approx 1.39 n\log_2 n$ (@eq-salgo-qs), so no input is bad on average, but an unlucky sequence of random choices can still be quadratic; the guarantee comes only from a fallback such as introsort's heapsort (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a7).
:::

**5. [M] How many comparisons does merging two sorted runs of lengths $p$ and $q$ make, at least and at most? Give inputs that reach both bounds.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each comparison outputs one element, and the merge stops comparing when one run is empty. **At least $\min(p, q)$:** if every element of the shorter run is smaller than every element of the other, that run is used up after $\min(p,q)$ comparisons (for example $[1,2]$ and $[3,4,5]$: two comparisons). **At most $p + q - 1$:** the last element is always output without a comparison, and if the runs interleave perfectly ($[1,3,5]$ and $[2,4,6]$) every other element needs one, so $5$ comparisons. That is why sorted input is merge sort's best case (about half the comparisons) (@sec-salgo-a3-merge).
:::

**6. [M] Prove that merge sort makes at most $n\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ comparisons, and name the two properties beyond speed that make merge sort the sort for linked lists and for data on disk.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A merge of $m$ elements makes at most $m - 1 < m$ comparisons. The subarrays at one level of the recursion tree are disjoint, so the merges of one level make fewer than $n$ comparisons together, and there are $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ levels of merges (the sizes halve, rounding up), so fewer than $n\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ in total. (1) The merge needs only **sequential access**: it reads both runs front to back, so on a list it relinks `next` pointers (@sec-salgo-p1-c) and on disk it streams. (2) It **combines independently sorted runs**, so a file too big for memory can be sorted in chunks and then merged (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-p4).
:::

**7. [M] In the classic Hoare partition with the pivot value taken from `a[(lo+hi)//2]`, show that the returned index $j$ satisfies $lo \le j < hi$, so both recursive calls are on strictly smaller ranges. What goes wrong with the pivot taken from `a[hi]`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $m = \lfloor (lo+hi)/2 \rfloor < hi$ when $lo < hi$. In the first round $i$ stops at some index $\le m$ (because `a[m]` $= x$ is not $< x$) and $j$ stops at some index $\ge m$. If $i \ge j$ already, then $i = j = m < hi$. Otherwise the two are swapped and the loop continues, and every later stop of $j$ is strictly below the previous one, so the final $j < hi$; symmetrically $j \ge lo$. With $x = $ `a[hi]` on input like $[1, 2]$: $i$ stops at index $1$, $j$ stops at index $1$, and the function returns $j = hi$, so the call on `[lo..j]` is the whole range again and the recursion never ends (@sec-salgo-a4-hoare).
:::

**8. [M] How many comparisons does the three-way partition make on $n$ equal keys, and how many does Lomuto's quicksort make? Explain the difference in one sentence.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Three-way: each element is tested once against `<` and once against `>`, then joins the `== x` block, so $2n$ comparisons and the sort is finished (the test in @sec-salgo-a4 measures exactly $2 \cdot 256$). Lomuto: every element is $\le x$, so each partition peels off only the pivot and the total is $\binom n2$. The three-way partition puts all keys equal to the pivot in their final place at once and never recurses into them (@sec-salgo-a4-hoare).
:::

**9. [M] Show that quickselect with a random pivot does expected $O(n)$ work, and say when a size-$k$ heap is the better tool.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Call a pivot good if it falls in the middle half of the current range; then the kept side has at most $\tfrac34$ of the elements. Each pivot is good with probability $\tfrac12$, so the expected number of partitions until the range shrinks by a factor $\tfrac34$ is $2$, each costing at most the current size. The expected total is at most $2(n + \tfrac34 n + (\tfrac34)^2 n + \dots) = 8n$. A size-$k$ heap, $O(n\log k)$, is better when you need *all* top $k$ in order, when the data **streams** (quickselect needs everything in memory), or when you want a worst-case bound (@sec-salgo-a4-select, @sec-salgo-p4).
:::

**10. [M] Run the bottom-up heap build on `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]` (max-heap, 0-based). Write the array after each sift-down and count the swaps. Relate the count to node heights.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Internal nodes are indices $2, 1, 0$. Index 2 (value 3, children 6, 7): swap with 7 → `[1,2,7,4,5,6,3]`. Index 1 (value 2, children 4, 5): swap with 5 → `[1,5,7,4,2,6,3]`. Index 0 (value 1, children 5, 7): swap with 7 → `[7,5,1,4,2,6,3]`; then at index 2 (children 6, 3): swap with 6 → `[7,5,6,4,2,1,3]`. Four swaps, which equals the sum of the heights of the internal nodes ($1 + 1 + 2$): an increasing array is the worst case for a max-heap build, every value sinks to the bottom. In general the swaps are at most the sum of all heights, which is less than $n$ (@sec-salgo-a5-build).
:::

**11. [M] Show that heapsort is not stable with the smallest possible input, and explain how to make *any* sort stable. What does it cost?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Two equal keys $[0_a, 0_b]$: the build changes nothing (the root is not smaller than its child), then the first extraction swaps the root with the last element, giving $[0_b, 0_a]$. To make any sort stable, sort pairs $(\text{key}, \text{input index})$: equal keys then compare by index, so their input order is kept. It costs $O(n)$ extra memory for the indices and a slightly slower comparison; the time bound is unchanged (@sec-salgo-a5, @sec-salgo-a6-stable).
:::

**12. [M] Build a two-key order by sorting twice (secondary key first, then primary) and say which sorts make this work and which silently break it. Give the one-line Python equivalent.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only a **stable** second pass works: the primary-key pass must keep the secondary order inside groups of equal primary key. Insertion sort, merge sort, Timsort (Python `sorted`) and C++ `stable_sort` are fine; quicksort, heapsort, selection sort and C++ `std::sort` may scramble the groups (the test in @sec-salgo-a6-stable finds such a case for heapsort). One line: `sorted(recs, key=lambda r: (r.primary, r.secondary))` (@sec-salgo-a6-stable).
:::

**13. [H] Prove the comparison lower bound $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil$ and the estimate $\log_2(n!) \ge \tfrac n2\log_2\tfrac n2$. Then identify exactly which assumption counting sort breaks.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A comparison sort on inputs of size $n$ is a binary decision tree whose leaves are its possible outputs; two different input permutations must reach different leaves (the same moves cannot sort both), so there are at least $n!$ leaves. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, so $2^h \ge n!$ and the worst case $h \ge \log_2(n!)$. For the estimate, $n! \ge n(n-1)\cdots(\lceil n/2\rceil) \ge (n/2)^{n/2}$, so $\log_2(n!) \ge \tfrac n2\log_2\tfrac n2$. Counting sort breaks the "only comparisons" assumption: `cnt[x] += 1` uses $x$ as an index, a $k$-way branch on the key's value, so there is no binary decision tree (@sec-salgo-a6-bound, @sec-lts).
:::

**14. [H] Prove that even the *average* number of comparisons over all $n!$ inputs is at least $\log_2(n!)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let some leaves of a binary tree be at depths $d_1, \dots, d_L$. Kraft's inequality says $\sum_\ell 2^{-d_\ell} \le 1$ (start with weight $1$ at the root and split it equally between the two children at every internal node; each leaf receives exactly $2^{-d}$). The function $2^{-x}$ is convex, so by Jensen's inequality $2^{-\bar d} \le \frac1L\sum_\ell 2^{-d_\ell} \le \frac1L$, where $\bar d$ is the average depth. Hence $\bar d \ge \log_2 L$. Apply this to the $L = n!$ leaves reached by the $n!$ input permutations (each reaches its own leaf, and a subset of the leaves still satisfies Kraft's inequality): their average depth, which is the average number of comparisons over all inputs, is at least $\log_2(n!)$ (@sec-salgo-a6-bound).
:::

**15. [H] Introsort switches to heapsort after $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ levels and finishes with one insertion-sort pass over blocks of at most 16. Explain what each stage buys and prove the worst case is $O(n\log n)$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Quicksort gives the fast average and good cache behaviour; the depth cap catches runs of bad pivots and hands the block to heapsort, which is $O(m\log m)$ worst case in place; the insertion pass avoids recursion overhead on tiny blocks. Proof: each of at most $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ partition levels costs $O(n)$ across its disjoint blocks; the heapsort calls are on disjoint blocks, $O(n\log n)$ together; after the loop every element is within its block of at most 16, which is in its final position relative to other blocks, so the final insertion sort makes fewer than $16$ shifts per element, $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a7).
:::

**16. [H] Timsort reverses only *strictly* descending runs, and only ever merges two *neighbouring* runs on its stack. Show with small examples why each rule is needed for stability.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**Strict runs.** If descending runs were allowed to contain ties, $[2_a, 2_b, 1]$ would count as one descending run and be reversed to $[1, 2_b, 2_a]$, swapping the equal keys. With the strict rule the descending scan stops at the tie: $2_a, 2_b$ is a (non-decreasing) ascending run and is left as it is. **Neighbours only.** A merge outputs equal keys of its left input before those of its right input, which is correct only if the left input lies entirely before the right input in the array. Take runs $A = [1_a, 2]$, $B = [0, 1_b]$, $C = [1_c, 3]$ in that order. Merging $A$ with $C$ first gives $[1_a, 1_c, 2, 3]$, and merging that with $B$ outputs $1_a, 1_c, 1_b$: the input order $a, b, c$ is lost. Merging only neighbours keeps every pending run a contiguous block of the input, so every merge has its left input before its right input (@sec-salgo-a8).
:::

**17. [M] Compute Timsort's classic `minrun` for $n = 63$, $n = 1000$ and $n = 2112$, and explain why `minrun` is chosen so that $n / \text{minrun}$ is close to a power of two.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n = 63 < 64$: `minrun` $= 63$, a single binary insertion sort. $n = 1000 = 1111101000_2$: the top six bits are $111110_2 = 62$, and a lower bit is set, so `minrun` $= 63$ (giving 16 runs of about 63). $n = 2112 = 100001000000_2$: top six bits $100001_2 = 33$, no lower bit set, so `minrun` $= 33$ and $2112 = 64 \cdot 33$ splits into exactly 64 runs. On random data almost every run is boosted to exactly `minrun`, so the merge tree is perfectly balanced when the number of runs is a power of two; a count just above a power of two would leave one tiny run to be merged with a huge one at the end, which wastes copies (@sec-salgo-a8).
:::

**18. [M] Choose between merge sort and quicksort for (a) objects too big to fit in memory, (b) a linked list, (c) an array of integers where you want the fastest typical case, (d) counting inversions.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) Merge sort: sort chunks, then stream-merge the sorted runs with a heap of heads (@sec-salgo-p4). (b) Merge sort by relinking; quicksort needs swaps at arbitrary positions (@sec-salgo-p1-c). (c) Quicksort, in its introsort form: in place, cache-friendly, smallest constant (@sec-salgo-a7). (d) Merge sort: its merge exposes how the two halves compare, which is exactly what an inversion count needs (@sec-salgo-p2-a).
:::

**19. [M] In @sec-salgo-p2-b the answer credits a left element with `j`, the number of right-half elements already merged. Explain precisely why `j` equals the number of smaller elements to its right *that lie in the other half*.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two runs are the left and right halves of an original index range, so every right-half element has a larger original index than every left-half element. A right element is merged before a given left element exactly when it is strictly smaller (ties take the left first), so at the moment the left element is emitted, the `j` right elements already output are exactly the smaller ones from the right half. Pairs within the same half were credited deeper in the recursion (@sec-salgo-p2-b).
:::

**20. [M] @sec-salgo-p2-c counts pairs with `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]`. Why does a single forward pointer `j` tally all crossings between two sorted halves, and where does overflow hide?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With both halves sorted ascending, as the left value grows, the set of right values with $2 \cdot \text{right} < \text{left}$ can only grow, so `j` only moves forward and `j - mid` is the size of that set: $O(n)$ per level. Overflow hides in `2 * nums[j]` when `nums[j]` is near $\pm 2^{31}$; compute in `long long` (@sec-salgo-p2-c).
:::

**21. [M] In @sec-salgo-p3-b, why is binary search on the *value* valid when the matrix cannot be indexed by rank, and why does the "enough" branch set `hi = mid` rather than `mid - 1`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
"How many cells are $\le x$" is monotone in $x$, so the smallest $x$ with count $\ge k$ is well defined and binary search finds it; that $x$ is a cell value, because the count only changes at cell values, so it is the $k$-th smallest. `hi = mid` keeps `mid` itself as a candidate: it may be exactly the answer, and `mid - 1` could skip it (@sec-salgo-p3-b).
:::

**22. [E] You must return the $k$ closest points in any order. Why is sorting all points $O(n\log n)$ but a max-heap of size $k$ $O(n\log k)$, and when does the heap stop paying off?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The heap never holds more than $k$ elements, so each push or pop costs $O(\log k)$, for $O(n\log k)$ in total; it evicts the farthest point whenever it grows past $k$. When $k$ is a constant fraction of $n$, $\log k \approx \log n$ and the heap gains nothing over a sort, while quickselect's expected $O(n)$ then wins (@sec-salgo-p4-a).
:::

**23. [M] @sec-salgo-p4-b keeps a min-heap of the $k$ largest values. Prove that its root is the $k$-th largest, and explain why the admission test can be `val > root` (strict).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The heap holds exactly the $k$ largest values seen so far, so its minimum, the root, is the $k$-th largest. A new value changes the top-$k$ multiset only if it is larger than the root; a value *equal* to the root would replace it with an identical value and change nothing, so skipping it is correct and saves work (@sec-salgo-p4-b).
:::

**24. [M] LC 937 can be solved by sorting only the letter-logs, or by one stable sort with a sentinel key. Give the sentinel key and explain why C++ must use `stable_sort` for the one-sort version.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Key $=$ `(is_digit, content if letter else "", identifier if letter else "")`. All digit-logs get the same key, so they tie, and a *stable* sort keeps tied items in input order, which is the requirement. `std::sort` is unstable (introsort), so it may reorder the tied digit-logs; `std::stable_sort` keeps them (@sec-salgo-p5-a).
:::

**25. [M] For @sec-salgo-p5-b, sort `(attack, defense)` both ascending and give a concrete input on which the right-to-left sweep then counts a character as weak by mistake. What does sorting defense descending change?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $[[5,1],[5,5],[6,0]]$. Both ascending: $[[5,1],[5,5],[6,0]]$; sweeping right to left, `best` becomes $0$, then $5$ at $[5,5]$, and $[5,1]$ is counted weak because $1 < 5$, but $[5,5]$ has the *same* attack, and the only larger attack, $[6,0]$, has smaller defense, so $[5,1]$ is not weak. With defense descending inside equal attacks the order is $[[5,5],[5,1],[6,0]]$: an equal-attack neighbour to the right always has *smaller or equal* defense, so it can never raise `best` above an equal-attack row's defense; only strictly larger attacks can (@sec-salgo-p5-b).
:::

## Interview questions

<!-- Copied into the Question Bank (quiz mode) by gen_book.py. Keep the shape exactly: a bold line
     starting "**N. " with the question, then one collapsed "Answer" callout. Answers may cite @sec-… -->

**1. Name five comparison sorts and give each one's time, extra space and stability.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Insertion: $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(n)$ best, $O(1)$ space, stable. Selection: $\Theta(n^2)$ always, $O(1)$, not stable. Merge sort: $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, $O(n)$, stable. Quicksort: $O(n\log n)$ expected, $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(\log n)$ stack, not stable. Heapsort: $O(n\log n)$ worst, $O(1)$, not stable (@sec-salgo-a9).
:::

**2. Why is quicksort $O(n^2)$ on sorted input with a last-element pivot, and what are the standard fixes?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The last element of a sorted range is its maximum, so every partition splits $n-1 \mid 0$ and the costs add up to $\binom n2$. Fixes: a random pivot (expected $O(n\log n)$ on every input), median-of-three, and introsort's heapsort fallback after a depth limit (a guarantee). Separately, a three-way or Hoare partition fixes the all-equal-keys blow-up (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a7).
:::

**3. What makes merge sort $\Theta(n\log n)$ in the worst case while quicksort is only $O(n\log n)$ on average?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge sort's split is input-independent (always the middle), so its recursion tree always has $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ levels of $O(n)$ work. Quicksort's split depends on the pivot's rank, which can be extreme again and again, giving $n$ levels. Balanced by construction versus balanced by luck (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-a4).
:::

**4. Why is quicksort usually faster than merge sort and heapsort in practice, even though all three are $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its inner loop is a sequential scan that compares with one pivot held in a register and moves few elements; it works in place, so it touches less memory and uses the cache well. Merge sort moves every element at every level and needs a buffer; heapsort jumps between $i$ and $2i+1$, which is cache-unfriendly, and makes about twice as many comparisons. The expected $1.39\,n\log_2 n$ comparisons of random-pivot quicksort are a small price for that (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a5).
:::

**5. How do you keep quicksort's stack depth $O(\log n)$ even in its worst case?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Recurse into the smaller side and loop (tail-iterate) on the larger side. The smaller side has at most half the elements, so each nested call at least halves the size and the depth is at most $\log_2 n$; time can still be quadratic, but the stack cannot overflow (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis).
:::

**6. State the $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound and its hypothesis. How do counting and radix sort escape it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Any comparison sort makes at least $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil = \Theta(n\log n)$ comparisons in the worst case (and on average): its decision tree needs $n!$ leaves and a binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$. The hypothesis is that the algorithm learns about keys only through pairwise comparisons. Counting and radix sort use key values as array indices, which is not a comparison, so they can run in $O(n + k)$ (@sec-salgo-a6-bound, @sec-lts).
:::

**7. Why is building a heap $O(n)$ and not $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Bottom-up building sifts each node down at most its height, and most nodes are near the bottom: about $n/2$ leaves cost nothing, $n/4$ nodes cost one level, $n/8$ cost two, and so on. The sum $\sum_h \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} h$ is less than $n$. Only repeated pushes (sift-up from the bottom for each new element) cost $O(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a5-build).
:::

**8. What is a stable sort, why does it matter, and which standard sorts are stable?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Stability keeps equal-key items in input order. It matters for multi-key sorting by successive passes, for keeping a group in its original order (LC 937's digit-logs), and for predictable output. Python's `sorted` and `list.sort` (Timsort) and C++ `std::stable_sort` are stable; C++ `std::sort` is not. Any sort becomes stable if it sorts `(key, index)` pairs (@sec-salgo-a6-stable, @sec-salgo-p5-a).
:::

**9. What do `std::sort` and Python's `sorted` actually run?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`std::sort` (in GCC's libstdc++) is introsort: median-of-three quicksort with a recursion depth limit of $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, a heapsort fallback when the limit is hit, and a final insertion sort over blocks of at most 16; worst case $O(n\log n)$, not stable. `sorted` is Timsort: natural runs (strictly descending ones reversed), short runs extended to `minrun` by binary insertion sort, a stack of runs merged with a balance rule, galloping merges; stable, $n - 1$ comparisons on sorted input, $O(n\log n)$ worst case (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8).
:::

**10. How do you count inversions in $O(n\log n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge sort with a counter. Pairs within a half are counted recursively; for the pairs across the halves, when a right-half element is output before the left-half elements still waiting, it forms an inversion with each of them, so add their number. Both halves are sorted, so this is linear per merge. Sort indices instead of values to get per-element counts (@sec-salgo-p2-a, @sec-salgo-p2-b).
:::

**11. Find the $k$-th largest element without sorting. Give the algorithm, its cost and the alternative for a stream.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Quickselect: partition around a random pivot and continue only into the side that contains index $n - k$; expected $O(n)$, in place, worst case $O(n^2)$ (median of medians or introselect make it linear in the worst case). For a stream, keep a min-heap of the $k$ largest: $O(\log k)$ per element, the root is the answer (@sec-salgo-a4-select, @sec-salgo-p3-a, @sec-salgo-p4-b).
:::

**12. Why is merge sort, not quicksort or heapsort, the sort for a linked list?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A list has no random access: heapsort's children $2i+1, 2i+2$ cannot be reached cheaply, and quicksort's partition swaps elements at arbitrary positions. Merge sort splits with a slow/fast walk and merges by relinking `next` pointers, with no copying; done bottom-up it needs only $O(1)$ extra memory (@sec-salgo-p1-c).
:::

**13. When do you keep a heap instead of sorting?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When you need the extreme, or the $k$ extremes, repeatedly but never the full order: top-$k$ ($O(n\log k)$ instead of $O(n\log n)$), running medians, priority scheduling, $k$-way merging, and anything streaming. Extracting *all* $n$ elements from a heap is heapsort, $O(n\log n)$, so the win comes only from extracting or keeping far fewer than $n$ (@sec-salgo-a5, @sec-salgo-p4).
:::

**14. How would you sort 100 GB of records on a machine with 8 GB of memory?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
External merge sort. Pass 1: read the file in chunks that fit in memory, sort each chunk (any in-memory sort), write it out as a sorted run: about 13 runs. Pass 2: merge all runs at once with a min-heap holding the current head of each run, reading and writing sequentially with large buffers. If there are too many runs for one pass, merge them in groups. Merge sort fits because the merge reads its inputs strictly in order (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-p4).
:::

**15. Insertion sort is $O(n^2)$. Why do production sorts still use it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its cost is $O(n + \text{inversions})$ with a tiny constant: for blocks of a few dozen elements, or data that is nearly sorted, it beats the $n\log n$ sorts and their overhead. Introsort finishes blocks of at most 16 with one insertion pass, and Timsort extends short runs with binary insertion sort, which needs only $O(\log n)$ comparisons per element (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8).
:::

**16. How does selection sort differ from insertion sort in what it minimises?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Insertion sort minimises work on nearly sorted input: $O(n + \text{inversions})$ comparisons and moves. Selection sort always makes $\binom n2$ comparisons but at most $n - 1$ swaps, so it minimises writes, which matters when moving an element is expensive (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a2).
:::

**17. For "count pairs with $a_i > 2a_j$, $i < j$", give the brute force, the faster method and the subtle bug.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Brute force: test all pairs, $O(n^2)$. Faster: merge sort with a separate cross-count pass before each merge; both halves are sorted, so one forward pointer counts the pairs in $O(n)$ per level, $O(n\log n)$ in total. Bug: `2 * a[j]` overflows 32-bit integers for values near $2^{31}$; use 64-bit (@sec-salgo-p2-c).
:::

**18. Why does Timsort make only $n - 1$ comparisons on an already sorted list, and does that contradict the lower bound?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Run detection compares each element with its predecessor once; on sorted input that finds a single run of length $n$ with $n - 1$ comparisons, and there is nothing to merge. It does not contradict the lower bound, which is about the *worst* (or average) input: an adaptive sort may be fast on easy inputs as long as some inputs still cost $\Omega(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a8, @sec-salgo-a6-bound).
:::

## Summary

<!-- The callout-important below is copied into the Cheat Sheets appendix: make it stand alone. -->

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Insertion** `while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j+1] = a[j]; j -= 1`; $O(n + \text{inversions})$, in place, stable (@sec-salgo-a1).
- **Selection** `swap(a[i], a[argmin a[i..]])`; $\binom n2$ comparisons, $\le n-1$ swaps, not stable (@sec-salgo-a2).
- **Merge** sort the halves, merge taking the left head on ties (`L[i] <= R[j]`); $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, $O(n)$ extra, stable; bottom-up needs no recursion (@sec-salgo-a3).
- **Quicksort** random pivot; Lomuto (`a[j] <= x` grows the left region), Hoare (two fingers, middle pivot), or three-way `< == >`; expected $2n\ln n$ comparisons; recurse on the smaller side (@sec-salgo-a4).
- **Quickselect** partition, keep only the side with index $t$; expected $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a4-select).
- **Heap** children $2i+1, 2i+2$; sift-down swaps with the larger child; build bottom-up in $O(n)$; heapsort swaps the root to the end, $O(n\log n)$, $O(1)$ extra, not stable (@sec-salgo-a5).
- **Lower bound** $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil \ge \tfrac n2\log_2\tfrac n2$ comparisons, worst case and average (@sec-salgo-a6-bound).
- **Libraries** introsort = quicksort + depth limit $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ + heapsort + final insertion; Timsort = runs + minrun + merge stack + galloping, stable (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8).
- **Patterns** count across the merge (P2), select one rank (P3), bounded heap (P4), stable sort or designed tie-break (P5).
:::

- Every sort here keeps an invariant about a region that only grows: a sorted prefix, a sorted suffix, or "each call returns a sorted permutation" (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-a5).
- Insertion sort's cost is the number of inversions plus $n$; that makes it the best sort for tiny and nearly sorted inputs and the finisher inside hybrids (@sec-salgo-a1).
- Merge sort is balanced by construction: $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, stable, and its merge streams, counts crossings and relinks lists (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-p1-c, @sec-salgo-p2).
- Quicksort is balanced on average: with a random pivot every input costs about $1.39\,n\log_2 n$ comparisons; three-way partitioning handles duplicates and one-sided recursion selects a rank in expected $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a4, @sec-salgo-p3-a).
- Heapsort is selection sort with a heap: $O(n\log n)$ worst case in $O(1)$ memory; the bounded heap is the top-$k$ and streaming workhorse (@sec-salgo-a5, @sec-salgo-p4).
- No comparison sort beats $\log_2(n!)$ comparisons on its worst or average input; adaptive sorts are fast on easy inputs without contradicting this (@sec-salgo-a6-bound).
- Library sorts are hybrids: introsort guarantees the worst case, Timsort exploits runs and is stable; know which one your language runs (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8).
- Stability and tie-break direction are design decisions, not details; they decide whole problems (@sec-salgo-p5).

## Further reading

- [Sedgewick & Wayne, *Algorithms* (4th ed.), chapter 2 site](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/20sorting/) — elementary sorts, mergesort, quicksort with three-way partitioning, and heapsort, with Java code and visual traces (@sec-salgo-a1 to @sec-salgo-a5).
- [Tim Peters, `listsort.txt` (CPython source)](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Objects/listsort.txt) — the design notes of Timsort: runs, minrun, the merge policy (now powersort), galloping and its measurements (@sec-salgo-a8).
- [Wikipedia — Introsort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Introsort) — Musser's hybrid of quicksort, heapsort and insertion sort, with references to the original paper and to library implementations (@sec-salgo-a7).
- [cppreference — `std::sort`](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/sort) — the complexity guarantee, the lack of stability and the strict-weak-ordering requirement on the comparator (@sec-salgo-a7).
- [Python Sorting HOWTO](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html) — key functions, the documented stability guarantee, and multi-pass sorting (@sec-salgo-a6-stable, @sec-salgo-p5).
- [V8 blog — Getting things sorted in V8](https://v8.dev/blog/array-sort) — why a JavaScript engine replaced its quicksort with Timsort, with a readable account of runs and galloping (@sec-salgo-a8).
- [Wikipedia — Quicksort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicksort) — Lomuto and Hoare partitions, pivot rules, the average-case analysis and its history (@sec-salgo-a4).
- [Competitive Programmer's Handbook (Laaksonen)](https://cses.fi/book/book.pdf) — chapter 3 on sorting in contests: the sorting lower bound, counting sort, and using the library sort with comparators.
